contents.html: 8.1. Track 1: AI Systems as the Target of Cybersecurity Incidents
contents.html_ja: 8.1. トラック 1: サイバーセキュリティインシデントの標的としての AI システム
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。33 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: The in-person cybersecurity breakout focused on incidents in which the AI system is itself the target or victim of a cybersecurity or information-security event. Participants identified AI systems as new targets and attack surfaces, including compromised or manipulated agents, credential harvesting and privilege escalation in agent environments, AI-assisted phishing, shadow AI deployments, AI-enabled vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and cloud-native ephemeral workloads that may disappear before investigators can understand what happened. Participants emphasized that core security practices (i.e., system hardening, benchmarking, logging, identity and access management) remain essential. However, these practices must be extended to agents, harnesses, models, AI-specific infrastructure, and non-human identities.
contents.html_ja: 対面のサイバーセキュリティ分科会は、AI システム自体がサイバーセキュリティまたは情報セキュリティ事象の標的または被害者となるインシデントに焦点を当てました。参加者は、AI システムを新たな標的および攻撃対象領域として挙げ、その例として、侵害または操作されたエージェント、エージェント環境における認証情報の収集と権限昇格、AI を利用したフィッシング、シャドー AI の展開、AI を利用した脆弱性の発見と悪用、調査担当者が何が起きたかを理解する前に消失しうるクラウドネイティブな一時的ワークロードを挙げました。参加者は、システムのハードニング、ベンチマーク、ログ記録、アイデンティティ・アクセス管理といった中核的なセキュリティ実務が引き続き不可欠であると強調しました。ただし、これらの実務は、エージェント、ハーネス、モデル、AI 固有のインフラストラクチャ、人間以外のアイデンティティにまで拡張しなければなりません。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。33 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: The virtual cybersecurity breakouts reinforced similar concerns. Participants highlighted risks associated with shadow MCP servers, “vibe-coded” applications created outside IT oversight, exposed API keys and credentials, data spills, insecure AI-generated code, and uncertain liability hand-offs among model developers, deployers, and users. Across these discussions, visibility emerged as the prerequisite for all later response activity. Organizations cannot apply threat modeling, identify stakeholders, preserve evidence, or respond effectively to systems that security teams do not know exist.
contents.html_ja: オンラインのサイバーセキュリティ分科会でも、同様の懸念が強調されました。参加者は、シャドー MCP サーバー、IT の監督外で作成された「バイブコーディング」アプリケーション、公開された API キーや認証情報、データ流出、安全でない AI 生成コード、モデル開発者、展開者、ユーザーの間での責任の引き継ぎの不確かさに伴うリスクを挙げました。これらの議論を通じて、可視性が、その後のあらゆる対応活動の前提条件として浮かび上がりました。組織は、セキュリティチームがその存在を知らないシステムに対して、脅威モデリングを適用することも、関係者を特定することも、証拠を保全することも、効果的に対応することもできません。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。33 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: Participants also stressed that AI incident response exposes a workforce and terminology gap between cybersecurity and AI communities. Cybersecurity practitioners and AI practitioners often use the same terms differently (e.g., “red teaming” may mean penetration testing to cyber professionals but guardrail bypass testing to AI professionals). Cyber responders may understand traditional artifacts, logs, and malware investigation but lack familiarity with the AI pipeline from data ingestion through model training, deployment, retrieval, inference, and agent tool use. This gap complicates triage, evidence collection, root-cause analysis, and coordination during incidents.
contents.html_ja: 参加者はまた、AI インシデント対応が、サイバーセキュリティと AI のコミュニティの間にある人材と用語のギャップを露呈させると強調しました。サイバーセキュリティの実務者と AI の実務者は、同じ用語を異なる意味で使うことがよくあります（例: 「レッドチーミング」は、サイバーの専門家にとってはペネトレーションテストを意味しうる一方、AI の専門家にとってはガードレールを迂回するテストを意味しうる）。サイバーの対応者は、従来のアーティファクト、ログ、マルウェア調査は理解していても、データの取り込みから、モデルの学習、展開、検索、推論、エージェントによるツール利用に至る AI パイプラインには不慣れな場合があります。このギャップは、インシデント中のトリアージ、証拠収集、根本原因分析、調整を複雑にします。

contents.html: 8.2. Track 2: Misuse, Malfunction, and Harm-Based Incidents
contents.html_ja: 8.2. トラック 2: 悪用、誤動作、危害に基づくインシデント
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。34 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: The in-person harm-focused breakout emphasized that AI incident prioritization depends heavily on context and consequence. Participants discussed categories of harm (e.g., privacy breaches, financial harm, discrimination, client-facing errors, infrastructure damage, property damage, rights-related harms, malicious use, agentic behavior) that may affect safety-critical environments. A recurring point was that a technically secure AI system can still create an AI incident if it produces incorrect outputs, enables unacceptable decisions, or causes harm in a specific operational context.
contents.html_ja: 対面の危害重視の分科会では、AI インシデントの優先順位付けが文脈と結果に大きく左右されることが強調されました。参加者は、安全性が重要な環境に影響しうる危害のカテゴリ（例: プライバシー侵害、金銭的危害、差別、顧客向けのエラー、インフラへの損害、財産への損害、権利に関連する危害、悪意ある使用、エージェント型の挙動）について議論しました。繰り返し出た論点は、技術的に安全な AI システムであっても、誤った出力を生成したり、受け入れがたい意思決定を可能にしたり、特定の運用上の文脈で危害を引き起こしたりすれば、AI インシデントを生じうるという点でした。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。34 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: Participants also discussed the difficulty of identifying AI incidents before human users recognize that something is wrong. AI systems can behave probabilistically, may not reproduce the same failure twice, and may be manipulated through rare, context-dependent, or adversarially selected inputs. Participants raised the possibility of AI-assisted or agentic defenses operating at machine speed, particularly in scenarios in which human responders cannot keep pace with automated attacks. At the same time, they recognized that governance, authorization, provenance, and accountability mechanisms are not yet mature enough to support fully automated response without careful safeguards.
contents.html_ja: 参加者はまた、人間のユーザーが何かがおかしいと気づく前に AI インシデントを特定することの難しさについても議論しました。AI システムは確率的に動作する場合があり、同じ故障を二度再現しないこともあり、まれな、文脈依存の、または敵対的に選ばれた入力によって操作される場合があります。参加者は、特に人間の対応者が自動化された攻撃に追いつけないシナリオにおいて、機械の速度で動作する AI 支援型またはエージェント型の防御の可能性を提起しました。同時に、ガバナンス、認可、来歴、説明責任の仕組みは、慎重な保護措置なしに完全自動化された対応を支えるにはまだ成熟していないことも認識しました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。34 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: The harm-focused discussion also underscored that existing taxonomies and frameworks do not always map neatly to AI harms. Participants noted that AI incidents may combine cybersecurity, privacy, safety, consumer protection, civil rights, and sector-specific regulatory concerns. This creates a need for crosswalks among existing frameworks and clearer guidance on how harm-based incidents should be categorized, prioritized, escalated, and remediated.
contents.html_ja: 危害重視の議論ではまた、既存の分類体系やフレームワークが AI の危害に常にうまく対応づけられるわけではないことも強調されました。参加者は、AI インシデントが、サイバーセキュリティ、プライバシー、安全性、消費者保護、公民権、分野固有の規制上の懸念を併せ持つ場合があると指摘しました。このため、既存のフレームワーク間の対応表と、危害に基づくインシデントをどのように分類し、優先順位付けし、エスカレーションし、是正するかについての、より明確なガイダンスが必要となります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。34 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: 8.3. Cross-Breakout Themes
contents.html_ja: 8.3. 分科会横断のテーマ
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。34 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: From policy to implementation. Participants emphasized the need for technical recommendations, controls, implementation examples, and operational playbooks that map high-level policy and frameworks to day-to-day engineering and incident response activities. Strategic frameworks (e.g., NIST AI RMF, CSF) were viewed as useful, but participants wanted more guidance on how to translate those frameworks into practical controls, procedures, and response actions.
contents.html_ja: 政策から実装へ。参加者は、高レベルの政策やフレームワークを日々のエンジニアリングやインシデント対応の活動に対応づける、技術的な推奨事項、制御、実装例、運用プレイブックの必要性を強調しました。戦略的なフレームワーク（例: NIST AI RMF、CSF）は有用と見なされましたが、参加者は、それらのフレームワークを実践的な制御、手順、対応行動に落とし込む方法について、さらなるガイダンスを求めました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。34 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: Logging, retention, and detection. Participants agreed that logs are essential but insufficient for AI incident response. Logs must be strategically selected, retained, protected, searchable, and paired with usable detection logic. Participants warned that collecting large volumes of logs without the ability to identify relevant signals can overwhelm analysts and produce false positives rather than actionable evidence.
contents.html_ja: ログ記録、保持、検知。参加者は、ログが AI インシデント対応に不可欠であるものの十分ではないという点で一致しました。ログは、戦略的に選択され、保持され、保護され、検索可能であり、使用可能な検知ロジックと組み合わされなければなりません。参加者は、関連するシグナルを特定する能力がないまま大量のログを収集すると、アナリストを圧倒し、実行可能な証拠ではなく誤検知を生み出しかねないと警告しました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。34 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: Privacy, compliance, and logging tension. Several participants highlighted a direct tension between the evidence needed for AI incident response and the privacy or compliance constraints that may limit evidence collection. The most useful logs for AI IR may include prompts, outputs, data access records, retrieved content, tool calls, and prompt-injection traces. Those same logs may contain personal data, regulated information, proprietary data, or other sensitive content subject to PCI, GDPR, DLP, retention, or privacy obligations. Organizations need guidance on how to preserve useful evidence while meeting privacy, compliance, and records management requirements.
contents.html_ja: プライバシー、コンプライアンス、ログ記録の緊張関係。複数の参加者が、AI インシデント対応に必要な証拠と、証拠収集を制限しうるプライバシーまたはコンプライアンス上の制約との間に、直接的な緊張関係があると指摘しました。AI IR にとって最も有用なログには、プロンプト、出力、データアクセス記録、取得されたコンテンツ、ツール呼び出し、プロンプトインジェクションのトレースが含まれる場合があります。これらのログには、個人データ、規制対象の情報、専有データ、その他、PCI、GDPR、DLP、保持、またはプライバシー上の義務の対象となる機微な内容が含まれる場合があります。組織には、プライバシー、コンプライアンス、記録管理の要件を満たしつつ、有用な証拠を保全する方法についてのガイダンスが必要です。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。34〜35 ページにまたがる全文が 1 ブロックにあることを原本で確認した。

contents.html: Asset and dependency management. AI asset management must extend beyond traditional hardware and software inventory. Participants identified the need to track deployed models, data sources, agents, harnesses, MCP servers, retrieval systems, identities, credentials, business functions, vendor dependencies, and downstream systems. Unknown or ungoverned AI systems (e.g., shadow AI tools, shadow MCP servers, vibe-coded applications) substantially increase response difficulty because responders may not know what exists, who owns it, what data it accesses, or what business process it supports.
contents.html_ja: 資産と依存関係の管理。AI の資産管理は、従来のハードウェアおよびソフトウェアの目録を超えて拡張されなければなりません。参加者は、展開済みのモデル、データソース、エージェント、ハーネス、MCP サーバー、検索システム、アイデンティティ、認証情報、業務機能、ベンダーへの依存、下流のシステムを追跡する必要性を挙げました。未把握または統制されていない AI システム（例: シャドー AI ツール、シャドー MCP サーバー、バイブコーディングされたアプリケーション）は、対応者が、何が存在するのか、誰が所有しているのか、どのデータにアクセスするのか、どの業務プロセスを支えているのかを把握できない場合があるため、対応の難しさを大幅に高めます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。35 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: Vendor, procurement, and value-chain constraints. Participants emphasized that many organizations do not fully control the AI systems they rely on. Model providers, resellers, cloud providers, managed service providers, API platforms, and third-party vendors may control logs, model documentation, technical artifacts, and remediation actions. Government and enterprise procurement channels may further limit what information can be compelled or obtained during an incident. This creates a need for contract language, audit rights, incident notification clauses, evidence commitments, and clear contact paths across the AI value chain.
contents.html_ja: ベンダー、調達、バリューチェーンの制約。参加者は、多くの組織が、自らが依存する AI システムを完全には管理できていないと強調しました。モデルプロバイダー、再販業者、クラウドプロバイダー、マネージドサービスプロバイダー、API プラットフォーム、サードパーティのベンダーが、ログ、モデルの文書、技術的アーティファクト、是正措置を管理している場合があります。政府およびエンタープライズの調達経路は、インシデント中に強制できる、または入手できる情報をさらに制限する場合があります。このため、AI バリューチェーン全体にわたる、契約条項、監査権、インシデント通知条項、証拠に関する取り決め、明確な連絡経路が必要となります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。35 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: Terminology and framework crosswalks. Participants noted the presence of inconsistent terminology and role definitions across NIST, ISO, the EU AI Act, MITRE, OWASP, CSET, the Coalition for Secure AI, and other frameworks. Rather than calling only for new definitions, participants asked for crosswalks that help organizations understand how existing definitions, roles, taxonomies, and incident categories relate to one another. This was viewed as especially important for organizations trying to align AI governance, cybersecurity, legal, compliance, and operational response functions.
contents.html_ja: 用語とフレームワークの対応表。参加者は、NIST、ISO、EU AI Act、MITRE、OWASP、CSET、Coalition for Secure AI などのフレームワークの間で、用語や役割の定義に一貫性がないことを指摘しました。参加者は、新たな定義を求めるだけでなく、既存の定義、役割、分類体系、インシデント分類が互いにどう関係するかを組織が理解する助けとなる対応表を求めました。これは、AI ガバナンス、サイバーセキュリティ、法務、コンプライアンス、運用上の対応の各機能を整合させようとする組織にとって、特に重要であるとみなされました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。35 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: AI transparency artifacts and provenance. Participants debated whether AI SBOMs, model cards, or other machine-readable transparency artifacts can support incident response. Some participants saw AI SBOMs as a potential way to standardize information about model versions, scaffolding, fine-tuning, and dependencies. Others were skeptical, noting that current SBOMs are often used for third-party risk questionnaires rather than actual incident analysis and that there is not yet consensus on what an AI SBOM should contain. Provenance tracking was also described as difficult once inputs, model behavior, and emergent system interactions are combined.
contents.html_ja: AI の透明性に関する成果物と来歴。参加者は、AI SBOM、モデルカード、その他の機械可読な透明性成果物がインシデント対応を支援できるかどうかを議論しました。一部の参加者は、AI SBOM がモデルのバージョン、スキャフォールディング、ファインチューニング、依存関係に関する情報を標準化する手段になり得ると考えました。一方で懐疑的な参加者もおり、現在の SBOM は実際のインシデント分析ではなく、サードパーティリスクの質問票に使われることが多いこと、AI SBOM に何を含めるべきかについて合意がまだないことを指摘しました。来歴の追跡も、入力、モデルの挙動、創発的なシステム間相互作用が組み合わさると困難になると述べられました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。35 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: Forensic correctness and AI artifacts. Breakout participants raised unresolved questions about how to prove that an AI system has been corrected after an AI-specific incident, such as data poisoning, model compromise, prompt injection, or unsafe agent behavior. Unlike traditional malware analysis in which investigators may identify a specific malicious file or signature, AI failures may be distributed across data, weights, prompts, retrieval systems, or agent workflows. Participants requested DFIR guidance on what AI artifacts investigators should collect while recognizing that NIST may need to provide broad artifact categories rather than prescribe proprietary vendor formats.
contents.html_ja: フォレンジックにおける是正の確認と AI の成果物。分科会の参加者は、データポイズニング、モデルの侵害、プロンプトインジェクション、安全でないエージェントの挙動といった AI 固有のインシデントの後に、AI システムが是正されたことをどう証明するかについて、未解決の問いを提起しました。調査員が特定の悪意あるファイルやシグネチャを識別できる従来のマルウェア分析とは異なり、AI の障害はデータ、重み、プロンプト、検索システム、エージェントのワークフローにまたがって分散している場合があります。参加者は、調査員がどの AI 成果物を収集すべきかについて DFIR のガイダンスを求めましたが、NIST が提供すべきなのは、ベンダー固有の独自形式を規定するものではなく、広い成果物の分類である可能性があることも認識していました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。35〜36 ページにまたがる全文が 1 ブロックにあることを原本で確認した。

contents.html: Business impact and area of effect. Responders need to understand what an AI system supports before an incident occurs. Participants stressed that an AI failure that affects manufacturing, medical diagnostics, billing, financial onboarding, aviation, critical infrastructure, or student-facing educational tools will require different escalation paths and containment decisions. AI asset documentation should include business functions, safety relevance, fallback procedures, acceptable disruptions, and potential downstream impacts.

contents.html: Machine-speed response and human governance. Participants repeatedly raised the concern that AI-enabled attacks or agentic failures may unfold faster than traditional human-centered response processes. However, they also recognized that automated or agentic defenses require governance, authorization, provenance, and accountability mechanisms that are not yet fully mature. Response models are needed to define what actions can be automated, what actions require human authorization, and how decisions are logged and reviewed.
contents.html_ja: マシン速度の対応と人間によるガバナンス。参加者は、AI を用いた攻撃やエージェント型の障害が、従来の人間中心の対応プロセスよりも速く進行し得るという懸念を繰り返し挙げました。しかし同時に、自動化された防御やエージェント型の防御には、ガバナンス、認可、来歴、説明責任の仕組みが必要であり、それらはまだ十分に成熟していないことも認識されました。どの行動を自動化できるか、どの行動に人間による認可が必要か、判断をどのように記録しレビューするかを定める対応モデルが必要です。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。36 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: Examples and learning resources. Participants requested practical case studies, best-practice repositories, tabletop scenarios, and examples of AI incident response in operational settings. This need was especially acute for smaller organizations that lack specialized AI security staff, legal resources, or internal tooling to develop AI-specific safeguards on their own. Participants viewed practical examples as necessary to help organizations conceptualize what AI incident response looks like in practice.
contents.html_ja: 事例と学習資源。参加者は、実践的なケーススタディ、ベストプラクティスのリポジトリ、机上演習のシナリオ、運用環境における AI インシデント対応の事例を求めました。このニーズは、AI に特化したセキュリティ要員、法務上の資源、社内ツールを持たず、AI 固有の保護策を自力で整備できない小規模な組織で特に切実でした。参加者は、AI インシデント対応が実際にどのようなものかを組織が具体的に思い描くうえで、実践的な事例が必要であるとみなしました。

contents.html: 9. Conclusion
contents.html_ja: 9. 結論
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。37 ページの原本画像と文字層で全文を照合した。

contents.html: The workshop established that SI incident management is not an abstract future problem. Organizations are already training, evaluating, and deploying SI systems that may be susceptible to compromise or take unintended actions while handling sensitive data, supporting decisions, automating processes, customer interactions, security operations, or critical business functions. Existing cybersecurity incident-response foundations remain indispensable, but SI introduces new challenges in observability, control, evidence, governance, the value chain, the speed of incident occurrence, identification, the assessment of harm, and response.
contents.html_ja: このワークショップは、SI のインシデント管理が抽象的な将来の問題ではないことを確認しました。組織はすでに、機微なデータを扱い、意思決定を支援し、プロセス、顧客とのやり取り、セキュリティ運用、または重要な業務機能を自動化する際に、侵害を受けやすい、または意図しない行動をとるおそれのある SI システムを訓練、評価、展開しています。既存のサイバーセキュリティのインシデント対応の基盤は引き続き不可欠ですが、SI は、可観測性、制御、証拠、ガバナンス、バリューチェーン、インシデント発生の速度、識別、危害の評価、対応において、新たな課題をもたらします。

contents.html: The near-term opportunity is to translate the workshop’s findings to develop focused, connected, and implementation-ready guidelines that organizations can use. The guidelines should be built on existing in-practice documents and frameworks, such as SP 800-61r3, the upcoming document IR 8596, MITRE ATLAS, ISO/IEC incident-reporting work, the IQT Incident response guidebook, JCDC resources, SI incident databases, and other resources. NIST’s continued work will extend traditional cybersecurity incident response to address the operational realities of SI systems, including model life cycle events, telemetry, provenance, traceability, observability, forensic analysis, information sharing, and coordinated response across the SI value chain. The medium-term opportunity is to strengthen the ecosystem for incident data, documentation, reporting, and sharing. The long-term challenge is to resolve deeper research questions about telemetry, reproducibility, recovery, machine-speed response, attribution, and multi-party responsibility.
contents.html_ja: 短期的な機会は、ワークショップの成果を、組織が利用できる、焦点を絞り、相互に連携し、実装可能なガイドラインの策定へとつなげることです。ガイドラインは、SP 800-61r3、近く公表される IR 8596、MITRE ATLAS、ISO/IEC のインシデント報告に関する取り組み、IQT Incident response guidebook、JCDC の資料、SI インシデントデータベースなど、実務で使われている既存の文書やフレームワークを土台とすべきです。NIST は今後の取り組みで、従来のサイバーセキュリティのインシデント対応を拡張し、モデルのライフサイクルイベント、テレメトリ、来歴、トレーサビリティ、可観測性、フォレンジック分析、情報共有、SI バリューチェーン全体での連携した対応など、SI システムの運用上の実態に対応させます。中期的な機会は、インシデントのデータ、文書化、報告、共有のためのエコシステムを強化することです。長期的な課題は、テレメトリ、再現性、復旧、マシン速度の対応、帰属、複数当事者の責任に関する、より根本的な研究上の問いを解決することです。

contents.html: Recognizing how quickly SI is becoming a part of everyday life, business, critical infrastructure, and government services, NIST’s SI Incident Response work will focus on staying flexible and working closely with all stakeholders. As SI capabilities and risks evolve, NIST will engage with the community to identify new challenges and develop practical guidelines for emerging issues while also expanding and improving a broader set of clear, useful advice that keeps pace with technological advances, real-world experiences, and stakeholder needs. This approach ensures that guidelines remain relevant and effective amid rapid technological change.
contents.html_ja: SI が日常生活、事業、重要インフラ、政府サービスの一部になりつつある速さを踏まえ、NIST の SI インシデント対応の取り組みは、柔軟性を保ち、すべての利害関係者と緊密に連携することに重点を置きます。SI の能力とリスクが進展するにつれて、NIST はコミュニティと協力して新たな課題を特定し、新たに生じる問題に対する実践的なガイドラインを策定します。あわせて、技術の進歩、現実の経験、利害関係者のニーズに歩調を合わせた、明確で有用な助言のより広い集合を拡充し、改善していきます。この取り組み方により、急速な技術変化の中でも、ガイドラインが適切で有効であり続けることを確保します。

Abstract
Keywords
Reports on Computer Systems Technology

The NIST Workshop on SI Incident Management convened over 400 experts across government, frontier-model developers, cloud and cybersecurity providers, academia, standards organizations, and civil society to examine how organizations can prepare for, detect, handle, and recover from SI-related incidents. Motivated by federal directives, the workshop addressed the need for standards, response frameworks, and technical incident response capabilities as SI systems expand across critical infrastructure. To guide these efforts, participants framed SI incident management across two interrelated domains: cybersecurity attacks that target SI systems and incidents that stem from SI misuse, anomalous behavior, or severe operational malfunctions resulting in harm. Discussions and technical presentations highlighted the limitations of traditional, deterministic incident response life cycles when applied to probabilistic, autonomous, and deeply integrated SI systems. Participants emphasized critical operational needs, including reasoning-layer telemetry, non-human identity governance, authorization-scoped containment, clear evidentiary and reporting schemas, and coordinated responsibility across distributed SI value chains. This report synthesizes the core findings, practitioner insights, and actionable recommendations from the workshop to establish a strategic foundation for future NIST guidelines, operational playbooks, and updates to federal incident response frameworks.

Super intelligence (SI)1 is rapidly transforming the foundation of modern infrastructure and
4F

driving unprecedented advancements across public and private sectors. As SI systems become increasingly integrated into critical operations, they introduce a complex landscape of potential vulnerabilities, both as a target and as a source or facilitator. Unlike traditional deterministic IT systems, SI models are probabilistic, operate at autonomous machine-speed that vastly outpace human reaction times, and rely on complex development and algorithmic process. This new construction model means that SI systems are not only targets for new types of cyber threats (e.g., data poisoning, prompt injection, model inversion) but can also act as a source of harm through adversarial and non-adversarial malfunctions, hallucinations, or malicious misuse. Consequently, traditional incident response life cycles built for conventional software systems may fracture or be incomplete when applied to SI, making the updating of incident response in the presence of SI a priority.

The NIST Workshop on SI Incident Management was initiated following the federal AI Action Plan’s directive for NIST and the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) to collaborate with SI and cybersecurity stakeholders on developing standards, response strategies, best practices, and technical tools for SI incident management. The organizers described the event as the start of an ongoing process to evaluate existing practices, identify gaps, create a common vision for effective responses, and inform future updates and new resources to be produced by NIST.

This workshop was organized around incidents grouped broadly into two overlapping categories: cybersecurity attacks that target SI systems and incidents stemming from anomalous or unexpected behavior resulting from misuse or malfunction. Both require distinct response strategies, governance, and technical guidance:

Cybersecurity incidents that impact SI systems: Incidents that jeopardize the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of SI systems (e.g., SI models, agents, data, or supporting infrastructure), such as model theft, data poisoning, prompt injection, model inversion, supply-chain attacks, compromised agents, identity misuse, attacks on RAG pipelines, and others.

Incidents that can be caused by SI systems: Cases of misuse, malfunction, or high-stakes accidents involving SI systems leading to harm, such as unsafe outputs, hallucinations with operational consequences, malicious use leading to cybersecurity attacks, overreliance, harmful autonomous actions, misinformation, and impacts on financial systems or public safety.

The workshop combined formal presentations, a keynote, a session on attacks against SI systems, a session on misuse and malfunction, a survey of some existing guidelines, a panel on SI-agent roles and responsibilities, and concurrent breakout sessions with the attendees. The opening remarks reported participation by more than 400 in-person and online attendees, reflecting interest across government, industry, academia, civil society, and the cybersecurity and SI communities.

Keynote Address — “A Global Perspective on AI Incident Management: Risks, Responses, and Gaps,” by Prof. Neil Thompson (MIT FutureTech)

In his keynote address, Dr. Neil Thompson framed AI incident management as a problem of risk prioritization, evidence, organizational preparedness, and responsibility across the AI value chain. His keynote focused on three questions: which AI risks matter most, how companies are responding, and where major management gaps remain. He introduced the MIT AI Risk Initiative, including the AI Risk Repository, AI Risk Index, AI Mitigations Repository, AI Incident Tracking, and AI Governance Mapping. These resources are intended to help organizations identify AI risks, prioritize them, understand available mitigations, track real-world harms, and map relevant governance mechanisms.

Dr. Thompson discussed recent research from the project, which convened 272 professional and academic experts from 37 countries in a three-round survey to identify areas of agreement. These experts assessed AI risk by rating their concern, estimating probabilities for different levels of harm, identifying vulnerable actors and sectors, and assigning responsibility for mitigation. The results of the survey suggest that the most severe predicted AI risks over the next five years will be AI used for cyber attacks, weapons development, and mass harm; AI systems with dangerous capabilities; and competitive dynamics that may cause companies to compromise on safety and responsibility.

The expert assessment found substantial probabilities of severe or catastrophic outcomes, even when pragmatic mitigations were assumed. Based on current trajectories, experts assess that 18 of the 24 risks are more than 10 % likely to cause catastrophic outcomes (e.g., over 1 million deaths, more than $100 billion in financial losses) over the next five years. Even if pragmatic mitigations are adopted, experts still predict that five of the 24 risks are more than 10 % likely to cause catastrophic outcomes. These include dangerous AI capabilities (e.g., systems that can deceive, manipulate, or act autonomously in harmful ways), AI-enabled cyber attacks, environmental harm, inequality, unemployment, and power centralization (i.e., control over advanced AI becomes concentrated among a few firms or governments).

Experts also emphasized a mismatch between responsibility and vulnerability. Actors (e.g., general-purpose model developers, specialized developers, deployers, governance bodies) may have the greatest ability to reduce risk, while users and affected stakeholders may be the most vulnerable but have the least control. This gap creates a need for standards, contracts, reporting mechanisms, and coordinated governance across the AI value chain.

The presentation also reviewed how companies are responding to AI risks. MIT conducted a preliminary review of more than 550 public AI-related documents from 200 large market-cap global companies. The analysis identified apparent gaps between sectors’ assessed vulnerability and public evidence of company responses. Dr. Thompson emphasized that companies may have relevant internal practices that are not publicly documented and invited companies to validate the findings.
Define AI incidents, hazards, and near misses so that organizations can distinguish reportable incidents from routine model-performance issues.
Call to Action
Improve AI incident reporting beyond voluntary disclosures and media reports while protecting sensitive information.
Prioritize high-severity risks, especially AI-enabled cyber-attacks, weapons development, dangerous capabilities, and unsafe competitive dynamics.
Clarify responsibility across the AI value chain, including infrastructure providers, model developers, deployers, users, affected stakeholders, and governance actors.
Address the mismatch between responsibility and vulnerability through standards, contracts, governance mechanisms, and information-sharing structures.
Develop risk-specific mitigation guidelines that help organizations select practical controls based on sector, risk type, cost, and feasibility.
Prepare for serious failures and misuse with a special focus on agentic systems as well as multi-party incidents that require coordinated responses.
Support joint investigations and information sharing when incidents span multiple actors across the AI ecosystem.
4. Session — “AI Under Attack: Incident Response for AI Systems”
4.1. AI Under Attack: Where Your IR Life Cycle Cracks for Agentic Systems, by Kyriakos (Rock)
Lambros (Zenity)

This session was introduced by Craig Schlenoff and focused on the cybersecurity-centric aspects of AI incidents and the technical realities of defending AI assets as operational infrastructure, spanning training pipelines, models, inference endpoints, vector stores, agent toolchains, and downstream integrations. The session examined how traditional incident response assumptions are strained by AI-specific failure modes, including model inversion, data poisoning, adversarial prompt injection, model drift, and agentic systems whose containment depends on authorization scope rather than simple network segmentation.

Kyriakos (Rock) Lambros from Zenity spoke about severe structural “cracks” in the foundational incident response (IR) life cycle that could be exacerbated by the unique pressures of agentic systems. He warned the audience against two dangerous extremes: treating these systems as “just IT,” which ignores these fundamental cracks and leads to playbook failures, and assuming that AI requires a brand new model, which unnecessarily discards working methodologies. Instead, he urged practitioners to find the specific pressure points in their existing blueprints and patch them.

Lambros organized his fracture points around the four phases of incident response: Detection, Containment, Recovery, and Post-Incident Analysis. The first major fracture point Lambros identified is in the Detection phase, caused by the fact that the malicious “signal has moved up the stack.” Traditional security telemetry (e.g., network logs, endpoint agents, identity tracking) is largely blind to attacks like prompt injections, training-time data poisoning, and slow goal drift because they often masquerade as perfectly valid system interactions. Using the 2025 “EchoLeak” case as an anchor, he explained that harm now happens within the model’s reasoning layer long before any bad output triggers classical alerts. To mend this crack, he stressed the absolute necessity of implementing reasoning-layer telemetry.

The second and third fracture points disrupt the Containment and Recovery phases. Lambros challenged the traditional IR assumption that compromised assets can be safely hard-isolated or unplugged. Because AI agents are often deeply integrated into critical workflows, their potential effects are defined by their authorization scope rather than a simple network segment. Referencing a 2025 Replit Agent incident, he explained that containment must now rely on “time-to-revoke” primitives and “soft isolation.” Furthermore, recovery is complicated by the fact that surgically removing poisoned data (i.e., machine unlearning) is incredibly difficult, and some AI vulnerabilities simply cannot be patched in the traditional sense, a reality highlighted by the 2018 Amazon Recruiting and 2025 Anthropic GTG-1002 cases.

Finally, Lambros addressed the Post-Incident Analysis phase, which is heavily fractured by what he termed the “reproducibility envelope.” Unlike traditional malware, AI models are non-deterministic; a prompt that triggers a data leak today might yield a completely benign response tomorrow. This unpinned state makes investigating an attack impossible unless specific preparation work is done beforehand. To operationalize these fixes, Lambros left the audience with a strict 90-day action plan: within the first 30 days, organizations must add reasoning-layer logging to every AI deployment runbook; by day 60, they must measure and aggressively cut their time-to-revoke for agent authorizations; and by day 90, they must build comprehensive “soft isolation” playbooks to contain threats without breaking deeply integrated business systems.
Call to Action

Define reasoning-layer telemetry for AI incident response. Traditional network, endpoint, and identity telemetry is insufficient when the signal moves into the model or agent reasoning layer. NIST guidelines should define AI-specific forensic telemetry categories, including prompts, completions, intermediate reasoning or trace data, tool calls, authorization decisions, model/version information, and relevant agent states.

Shift containment from host isolation to authorization-scoped revocation. For agentic systems, the area of effect (sometimes called the “blast radius” by practitioners) is determined less by network location and more by the agent’s inherited authorization scope and downstream tools. NIST guidelines should recommend containment practices based on per-action authorization binding, capability scoping, tested kill-switch APIs, and measurable time-to-revoke for agent credentials and permissions.

Require the recovered system to produce both technical and governance evidence. AI recovery may require more than patching or rollbacks. Guidance should be developed to describe recovery outputs as both a remediated technical artifact and an updated governance package that demonstrates why the recovered system should be trusted after the incident.

Define a reproducibility envelope. AI systems can be stochastic, vendor-updated, tool-connected, and difficult to reproduce after the fact. A reproducibility-envelope specification must be defined using model versions, prompt sets, tool states, dependent service versions, seeds, retrieved context, logs, and relevant environment variables. This preparation work needs to be done before an incident, not only during post-incident analysis.

Practical readiness benchmark. Organizations should add reasoning-layer logging to AI deployment runbooks, measure and cut time-to-revoke for agent authorizations, and capture reproducibility-envelope specifications for production AI systems before they are needed.
4.2. Investigating Artificial Intelligence Attacks: A Framework, by James Perry (CrowdStrike)

James Perry, Global Vice President and Head of Incident Response at CrowdStrike, focused on the forensic challenge of investigating attacks against AI systems. His central message was that AI incident response will still need to answer the basic questions of who, what, when, where, and why. However, AI systems complicate each of these questions because the evidence needed to reconstruct actor behavior, data access, identity use, model behavior, and downstream system interactions is often missing, incomplete, ephemeral, or too voluminous to process in time.

Perry emphasized that traditional incident responders know how to investigate conventional endpoints, servers, cloud systems, and SaaS environments because they understand where the relevant logs, artifacts, and forensic evidence reside. By contrast, AI systems often do not preserve comparable evidence. When models are tampered with or AI systems are compromised, responders cannot simply image a disk, preserve the state, and reproduce the incident later. Hosted LLMs, self-hosted inference systems, agentic frameworks, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, orchestration layers, and downstream APIs all create different forensic visibility problems.

A major theme of Perry’s talk was the lack of reliable AI-native logging. He noted that many LLM deployments do not log prompts, responses, agent actions, the identities used to access data stores, or the specific data accessed. Without those records, investigators may be forced to operate using educated guesses rather than facts. Perry also highlighted the practical challenge of scale: even when logs exist, they may be so voluminous that organizations cannot store, retrieve, or analyze them quickly enough to meet legal, regulatory, and operational requirements.

Perry urged organizations and NIST to think in terms of a common investigative data model for AI. The required evidence should span hosted LLM platforms, self-hosted inference servers, frontier-model services, agentic frameworks, MCP servers, harnesses, and the connective tissue between them. He stressed that this data needs to be available in a common and machine-understandable format because investigations now need to operate at machine speed.

He closed by returning to the forensic questions that an AI investigation must answer: which identity, API key, or system component performed the action; what data was accessed; when the data was collected, trained on, retrieved, or returned; where the data went; and why the actor or system behaved as it did. He also identified several immediate practices, such as logging and retaining prompt and completion content by default where permissible, preserving the forensic traceability of collected data, avoiding the automatic destruction of ephemeral systems before evidence is captured, and standardizing timestamps so that investigative data can be correlated reliably across systems. Perry specifically identified timestamp standardization as a major practical issue and a concrete area where NIST could help.

Define AI forensic telemetry requirements. NIST guidelines should identify the minimum evidence needed to investigate AI attacks, including prompts and completions where permissible, agent actions, the identities and API keys used, the data stores accessed, retrieved content metadata, model and data version information, tool calls, MCP/harness activity, invocation logs, IP addresses, activity logs, and relevant compliance APIs.
Call to Action

Standardize a machine-readable AI investigation record. Perry’s strongest NIST-facing recommendation was to establish a common or machine-understandable format for AI investigative data across hosted LLMs, self-hosted inference servers, agentic frameworks, and AI orchestration layers.

Preserve prompt and completion content where legally and operationally feasible. In the Q&A, Perry recommended 30 days as a baseline retention period for prompt/completion content with longer retention when cost, complexity, and regulatory constraints allow.

Require forensic traceability of collected AI evidence. Organizations should know where evidence came from, who or what collected it, and whether it was collected by a human, agent, system process, or other mechanism. This is necessary for later legal, regulatory, or litigation-driven reviews.

Standardize timestamps across AI incident evidence. Perry made this one of his clearest practical asks for NIST since inconsistent time zones and timestamp formats consume excessive investigative effort, and AI-scale investigations require consistent, machine-readable timestamping.

Account for ephemeral and distributed AI infrastructure. AI incident guidelines should warn organizations not to destroy or auto-delete ephemeral systems, containers, agents, or cloud resources before evidence is captured. The framework should address how to preserve state and investigative artifacts from systems that may spin up, act, and disappear within seconds.

Robert Saul, General Manager of the Amazon Web Services (AWS) Customer Incident Response Team, focused on incident response preparation for AI systems. His message was pragmatic: AI does not require abandoning the classical incident response discipline, but it does require organizations to prepare differently because AI systems introduce new assets, identities, evidence sources, business dependencies, and containment trade-offs.

Saul argued that the best-performing incident response teams are those that have done the governance work before the incident. He identified three areas that separate good response from great response: non-human identity governance, pre-positioned telemetry, and containment decision frameworks.

First, Saul emphasized non-human identity governance. AI systems create and depend on service accounts, Application Programming Interface (API) keys, authentication tokens, pipeline credentials, orchestration secrets, and agent-to-agent trust relationships. These identities often do not appear in traditional IR asset inventories. When compromised, response teams may not know what the identity does, what permissions it has, how to revoke it, or what business function will break when the trust layer is removed. Saul argued in favor of maintaining a living inventory of AI-created non-human identities mapped to business functions, permissions, behavior baselines, owners, and tested revocation playbooks.
4.3. Incident Response Preparation for AI Systems, by Robert Saul

Second, Saul emphasized pre-positioned telemetry. This includes prompt/completion logs, model version history, training-data access, embedding queries, agent decision traces, and drift metrics. Saul stressed that logs should not merely be collected as technical artifacts; they should be mapped to investigation questions and the business functions they protect so that analysts can understand what they are defending.

Third, Saul emphasized containment decision frameworks. In AI systems, containment itself can cause damage. Killing an agent can corrupt downstream states; rolling back a model can break dependent services; and isolating a vector store can take down production. Saul recommended pre-built containment decision trees for AI components that are anchored in business functions. These decision trees should define available containment options (e.g., revoke, rollback, isolate, disable, fallback), cascading business effects, and approval authorities based on business impact.

Saul’s practical call to action was to start with one AI system and build its governance record by cataloging its non-human identities, mapping its data flows end to end, documenting its failure modes, and building one containment decision tree. His core message was that teams that respond well are not simply faster; they did the governance work when it was still boring.

Create AI system governance records. New guidelines should recommend that organizations maintain a living map for each significant AI system, including identities, data flows, failure modes, ownership, and business dependencies.

Inventory non-human identities as first-class IR assets. Guidance should treat service accounts, API keys, OAuth tokens, agent credentials, inter-service trust chains, pipeline credentials, and orchestration secrets as core assets for incident response preparation.

Map effect areas in business terms. Organizations should document areas of effect (i.e., “blast radius”) for each AI-created identity and component both in technical terms as well as in terms of affected business functions.

Pre-position AI-specific telemetry. Organizations should identify, collect, retain, and test AI evidence sources before an incident, including prompt/completion logs, model lineage, embedding queries, training-data access, agent traces, and drift metrics.

Build containment decision trees before incidents. For each important AI component, organizations should define containment options (e.g., revoke, rollback, isolate, disable, fallback), document cascading effects, and specify who has authority to accept the resulting business risk.

Run tabletop simulations with IR, ML, and business owners together. In addition to technical responders, Saul recommended practicing scenarios with the people who understand model behavior, business impact, and operational authority.
Call to Action
5. Session — Misuse and Malfunction: Understanding Emerging AI-Induced Incidents
5.1. AI Incident Database: The Next 6,173 AI Incident Reports, by Sean McGregor (AIID)

This session was chaired by Jon Boyens of NIST and examined “Misuse and Malfunction: Understanding Emerging AI-Induced Incidents.” The session shifted the workshop focus from AI systems as targets of attack to AI systems as sources, facilitators, or amplifiers of harm. It explored how organizations should understand and respond to AI-induced harms, including malicious misuse, non-adversarial malfunctions, hallucinations, and other frontier-model risks. Across the talks, the session emphasized the need to distinguish between information sharing, incident reporting, and incident response; to move beyond anecdotal incident narratives toward structured data and probabilistic risk measurement; and to develop practical response mechanisms for large-scale, cross-organizational GenAI incidents.

Dr. Sean McGregor, Executive Director of the AI Incident Database, spoke about how AI incident management must move beyond isolated anecdotes toward structured incident data, shared evidence practices, and measurable risk. Drawing on the AI Incident Database’s (AIID) first 6,173 incident reports, he emphasized that individual reports are useful but insufficient. The field needs data collection and modeling practices that can support learning, recurrence analysis, and risk measurement at scale.

McGregor began with an analogy to aviation safety, where accident and incident databases helped create a culture of systematic learning. He argued that AI needs a similar evidence base but noted that AI incidents are harder to define because they span intentional misuse, unintentional failures, security vulnerabilities, and broader harms. The AIID uses the term “incidents” because narrower terms (e.g., accidents, failures, vulnerabilities, threats, catastrophes, recalls) fail to capture intentional harms, are not event-oriented, or are too specific.

McGregor also emphasized the political and institutional difficulty of collecting AI safety data. Companies need accident and malfunction data to improve products, but the same data can create product-liability exposure. He noted that governments are extensive deployers of AI systems and have a first-party interest in collecting accidents, failures, and malfunctions related to the systems they use.

A central theme of the talk was that AI is too broad for any single organization or database to cover alone. McGregor argued that the field needs many databases that serve many purposes, are maintained by many organizations, share data, and use common fields where possible. He organized the landscape into three major categories: 1) security incidents in which the AI system is the target, 2) misuse involving intentional harms, 3) and accidents, failures, malfunctions, and hazards involving unintentional harms.

The latter part of the talk focused on moving from incident anecdotes to measurement. Dr. McGregor discussed nowcasting and pragmatic classification frameworks that estimate whether both harm and exposure are increasing or decreasing. This addresses the “denominator problem”: without understanding how widely a system or class of systems is deployed, incident counts alone cannot tell whether the technology is becoming safer or more dangerous on a “miles traveled” basis. He called on NIST to help clarify incident categories; develop common data fields; support hindcasting, nowcasting, and forecasting; advance incident management standards; and improve the naming of AI incident types.
